“A TEXAS FAMILY OF FOUR, THEIR NANNY, TWO CLOSE FRIENDS, AND TWO PILOTS.” — Heartbreaking details emerge following the catastrophic Palm Beach County Learjet 60 disaster, as sources confirm that prominent Austin tech founder Adam Robinson, his wife Helen, their two young toddlers, and five others perished when their private jet suffered a catastrophic in-flight failure en route to the Bahamas.

“The passengers aboard the private jet that crashed in Florida have been identified as a family of four from Texas traveling with their nanny and two close friends... Onboard the Learjet 60 were 44-year-old Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen, their two young children, and two close friends. The family had their nanny with them, and both pilots also died.”

— TMZ News / Family Sources

The Victims Aboard the Doomed Learjet
The Robinson Family: Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson (44), founder and CEO of Retention.com, his wife Helen, and their two toddler children tragically lost their lives together aboard the charter flight.

Family Friends and Caregiver: Joining the Robinson family were their private household nanny and two longtime close friends heading on a family vacation to the Bahamas.

The Flight Crew: The aircraft was piloted by Captain Jeff Gregory (55), a seasoned corporate aviator, alongside First Officer Nathalia Gadelha (20), a dedicated pilot who had earned her private license while attending high school in South Florida.

Key Developments in the Disaster
The Vacation Flight Route: The twin-engine Learjet 60 had originated in Austin, Texas, making an intermediate stop in Florida before setting course for the Bahamas over the Atlantic when it encountered heavy convective thunderstorms, severe turbulence, and rapid structural icing.

The Sudden Catastrophic Dive: Cockpit recordings captured the crew reporting manageable ice before declaring a sudden mayday, reporting that the aircraft had entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition descending in excess of 20,000 to 32,000 feet per minute.

NTSB In-Flight Breakup Findings: Briefings from the National Transportation Safety Board revealed that debris and structural components separated from the jet at altitude, with dashcam footage indicating the aircraft plunged without its horizontal stabilizer assembly.

“THE BALL IS IN THE U.S. COURT.” — Iran’s Foreign Ministry announces a conditional 48-hour proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt attacks on international shipping, demanding immediate reciprocal military de-escalation and economic guarantees from Washington as high-stakes backchannel negotiations continue in Doha.

“Iran is fully prepared to restore normal maritime navigation and guarantee safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz within 48 hours, but security cannot be unilateral. If Washington halts its strikes and meets our core sovereign conditions, this maritime standoff ends immediately. The ball is entirely in the U.S. court.”

 Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi

A Conditional 2-Day Reopening Plan: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi presented a structured 48-hour timeline under which Iranian naval forces and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fast-attack craft would stand down from maritime interdictions, allowing commercial tankers to resume transit through the 21-mile-wide chokepoint.

 Tehran’s diplomatic framework requires the United States to immediately halt retaliatory airstrikes, freeze planned operations against Iranian energy terminals, and establish formal security guarantees mediated through ongoing negotiations in Doha, Qatar.

The proposal follows weeks of escalating maritime warfare in which 11 commercial supertankers were struck or damaged by limpet mines, loitering munitions, and drone boats in the Strait of Hormuz, driving maritime insurance premiums to historic highs and threatening roughly 20% of the world's petroleum transit.

The 48-hour window presents a critical crossroads for the administration: defense hawks advocate continuing kinetic strikes to degrade Iran's anti-ship missile sites, while regional Gulf partners and economic advisors urge accepting a ceasefire framework to avert an international energy shock.

Accepting Tehran's terms risks signaling that maritime extortion yields diplomatic leverage, while rejecting the 48-hour off-ramp could trigger protracted naval combat across the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman.

Vulnerability of Global Supply Chains: With approximately 850 crude supertankers operating globally, prolonged closures or continuous mine warfare threaten global fertilizer, crude oil, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) distribution networks.

Testing Diplomatic Backchannels: The proposal marks the most direct engagement between Tehran and Washington since hostilities expanded, serving as a decisive litmus test for broader regional negotiations.

Two photographs, four years apart, tell the whole story of what war did to Evgeny Kobytev. In 1941 he was thirty, a trained Soviet artist, confident and full of life. Then Germany invaded, he went to the front, and he was taken prisoner. He spent years in German captivity — starvation, forced labor, brutality that k*lled millions of Soviet POWs.

When he came home in 1945, the young artist was gone. The man in the second photograph looks decades older, gaunt and weathered, his face carrying everything the camps took from him. But he had survived — and he picked up his brush again, spending the rest of his career painting what he had witnessed. His art, and those two photographs, remain a stark record of what endurance really costs.

“EVIDENCE INDICATES PARTS OF THE JET BROKE OFF BEFORE IMPACT.” — Federal investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board reveal that the doomed Learjet 60 that crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, likely suffered an in-flight structural breakup at altitude, aligning with dashcam video appearing to show the aircraft plunging nose-first without its T-tail horizontal stabilizer.

“There are indications the aircraft began breaking up prior to impact. We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site... We are asking anyone in the community who locates debris to contact local law enforcement immediately.”

— National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) Press Briefing in Palm Beach County

“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence... Mayday, mayday, we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute... We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute... We’re going to crash into the ground.”

— Cockpit transmissions broadcast over Air Traffic Control frequencies moments before impact

Aerodynamic & Forensic Breakdown
The In-Flight Breakup Finding: During their initial media briefing in Palm Beach County, NTSB investigators confirmed that the Learjet 60 began shedding components prior to striking the ground, officially expanding the search radius across residential neighborhoods miles away from the primary impact crater.

The Missing Horizontal Stabilizer: Close-up frame analysis of civilian dashcam footage captured seconds before impact appears to show the aircraft's T-tail fuselage cleanly sheared off, missing the entire horizontal stabilizer and elevator assembly that controls aircraft pitch.

Why Loss of the Stabilizer is Fatal: On swept-wing, T-tail jets like the Learjet 60, the horizontal stabilizer generates continuous downward aerodynamic force to counter the natural forward center of gravity. If the stabilizer separates due to severe structural flutter, pitch trim runaway, or aerodynamic over-stress, the aircraft immediately lawn-darts into a near-vertical terminal dive that is physically impossible to pull out of, regardless of pilot yoke input.

The Escalating Mayday Telemetry: Flight tracking telemetry and ATC recordings show the crew encountered severe weather and icing while climbing through 8,700 feet. The aircraft suddenly entered an uncontrollable overspeed condition, with vertical descent rates accelerating from 10,000 FPM past 32,000 FPM before the violent ground collision.

Key Investigation Priorities for the NTSB
Locating the Empennage Components: Ground teams are prioritizing the recovery of tail structure fragments, elevator control horns, and pitch trim actuators to determine whether failure was aerodynamic, mechanical, or structural.

Analyzing Trim Jackscrew Position: Recovery crews will inspect the horizontal stabilizer trim actuator jackscrew to determine if an uncommanded runaway pitch condition preceded the structural separation.

Evaluating Atmospheric Stress & Icing: Meteorologists and investigators are analyzing weather radar data to evaluate whether severe convective turbulence or structural ice accumulation induced catastrophic aerodynamic loading at cruise altitude.

When then-Pfc. Adlesperger and his squad approached a house on Nov. 10, 2004, in the treacherous city of Fallujah. They entered into one of the most difficult and dangerous battlefield situations: they faced an entrenched enemy in an urban setting, with an entrenched machine gun.

As they entered the house, a volley of insurgent fire and grenades rained down upon them, immediately killing Adlesperger’s point man and injuring two others. Without pause, Adlesperger took control and moved out front, despite receiving minor wounds. As Adlesperger began firing back from the point position, he became the main target of enemy fire – but, with most of his squad pinned down by insurgent fire, he had no choice but to push forward on his own.

Adlesperger single-handedly cleared the stairs to the rooftop, which allowed the unit to move injured Marines upstairs to receive medical attention. And as U.S. forces gathered for a major assault on the building, Adlesperger, still inside, began moving from one spot to another, eliminating enemies in close quarters or forcing them to move out of entrenched positions to areas where U.S. forces were waiting.

Finally, an assault vehicle broke through a wall on the main floor. Adlesperger rejoined his platoon and demanded to take point for the final attack on the entrenched machine gun. He entered the courtyard first and eliminated the final enemy at close range. By the end of the battle, Adlesperger was credited with having killed at least 11 insurgents.

One month later, Adlesperger was killed while clearing other houses in Fallujah. For his actions on Nov. 10, 2004, Adlesperger will be posthumously awarded the Navy Cross on April 13, 2007.

“EVERY CHILD DESERVES TO FEEL LOVED AND REMEMBERED, ESPECIALLY DURING THE HOLIDAYS.” — When I had Jen Lilley on the Shawn Ryan Show #314, we had an incredible conversation about the brutal realities facing children in the American foster care system. That conversation stuck with me, and I’m proud to support the life-changing work she’s doing through her Christmas Is Not Cancelled initiative.

“There are over 400,000 children in the U.S. foster care system right now, and so many of them enter homes carrying whatever few belongings they have in a black trash bag. When a child in foster care receives a brand-new toy or a backpack of their own, it sends a profound message: You are seen, you are not forgotten, and your life has purpose.”

 Jen Lilley, Actress, Co-Author of Called to Foster?, and Co-Founder of Christmas Is Not Cancelled

Through her nonprofit initiative Christmas Is Not Cancelled, Jen Lilley and her team partner with organizations like Toys for Tots to provide more than 20,000 brand-new toys and essential supplies to foster children and at-risk youth nationwide every holiday season.

 Foster youth frequently face sudden placements, separated siblings, and chronic instability. Providing brand-new, personalized holiday gifts ensures children never feel like an afterthought during what should be the most joyful time of the year.

 Alongside foster care expert Dr. John DeGarmo, Lilley authored Called to Foster?: An Honest Guide to Getting Started, providing families with transparent, practical guidance on navigating licensing, trauma-informed parenting, and adoption.

Beyond the holiday toy drive, the campaign delivers filled backpacks and educational supplies every summer, equipping foster students with the tools and confidence they need to succeed in school.

How You Can Help This Season
Sponsor a Holiday Toy: Visit the campaign to sponsor a brand-new toy or gift bundle directly for a child currently in foster care.

 Connect with licensed foster support networks in your community to donate essential clothing, duffel bags, and hygiene kits.

Picture it: pitch black, eight-foot waves, more than two dozen people scattered across the Pacific, and one young man in the water. Coast Guard rescue swimmer Josh Law, just twenty-four, was lowered from a helicopter before dawn on October 16 after a boat capsized roughly 140 miles off Baja California. Guided only by the searchlight sweeping the waves, he swam from survivor to survivor — turning them onto their backs, towing each one through the pounding surf to the rescue basket.

He stayed in that water for over an hour, long past the point of exhaustion, water filling his snorkel, and pulled sixteen people out alive. Sixteen families got their loved ones back because one swimmer refused to quit. That is what the job looks like when everything is on the line.

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties while serving in Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safe guard and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time.

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on, south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq.

When these IEDs exploded three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles.

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices.

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance.

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush.

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist.

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris, and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience.

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

In 1942, when more than 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced from the West Coast into internment camps, three farming families in California's Central Valley faced losing everything they had built. Their neighbor, a farmer named Bob Fletcher, refused to let that happen.

For three years he ran their farms as his own — working the land, paying the bills and taxes, keeping every operation alive — while enduring threats and hostility from people who hated what he was doing. Shots were even f*red at him. He never wavered. When the families came home in 1945, their farms were waiting for them, intact. In one of America's darkest chapters, one ordinary man quietly chose to do the right thing, and three families kept their futures because of it.

When the Civil War broke out, Mary Walker wasn't asking for permission. She was already a doctor, one of the very few women in America who could say that back in 1855. The Army told her women couldn't serve as surgeons. So she showed up anyway and worked for free.

She treated wounded Union soldiers in field hospitals, often close to the fighting. She'd cross into dangerous ground to care for civilians too, and in April 1864 that cost her. Confederate troops captured her and accused her of being a spy. She spent four months locked up in Castle Thunder prison in Richmond before she was traded back in a prisoner exchange.

In November 1865, President Andrew Johnson awarded her the Medal of Honor.

But her story didn't end neatly. In 1917, the government tightened the rules and took the medal back from her and hundreds of others. Mary's answer? She refused to return it. She wore it every single day until she died in 1919.

It took almost 60 more years, but in 1977 President Jimmy Carter restored her medal.

To this day, she is the only woman ever to receive the Medal of Honor.

She was stubborn, fearless, and way ahead of her time. And she never once backed down.

Rest easy, Dr. Walker. 🇺🇸

When the assault stalled under a wall of fire, he didn’t hesitate—he ran straight into the breach to protect his brothers and finish the mission.

Master Sergeant Joshua L. Wheeler, a legendary U.S. Army Delta Force (1st SFOD-D) operator who spent over two decades serving at the absolute spearhead of American special operations.

Starting his career in the 75th Ranger Regiment before earning his place in Delta Force, Wheeler deployed into combat an astonishing 14 times across Iraq and Afghanistan. He was the quintessential quiet professional: calm under pressure, master of his craft, and fiercely dedicated to the operators beside him.

On October 22, 2015, Wheeler was advising a joint strike force during a high-stakes night raid on an ISIS prison compound near Hawija, Iraq, where roughly 70 hostages faced imminent mass execution. When partner Kurdish forces were pinned down by heavy enemy small-arms fire and the assault began to falter, Wheeler refused to stand back. Breaking cover, he charged directly into the firefight, drawing enemy attention and rallying the assault force to breach the compound.

His decisive courage saved dozens of civilian lives, but cost him his own. MSG Wheeler became the first American service member killed in action fighting ISIS. He was posthumously awarded the Silver Star, adding to a lifetime of valor that included four Bronze Stars with "V."

A warrior who lived by the creed that the life of your teammate is worth more than your own.

Rest in Valhalla, Master Sergeant Wheeler. Never forgotten. 🇺🇸⚡🗡️🦅

She was twenty-five, thousands of miles from Gary, Indiana, doing the unglamorous work that keeps an air war alive. Marine Sergeant Jeannette L. Winters served with Marine Aerial Refueler Transport Squadron 352 out of Miramar, flying KC-130s — hauling fuel, cargo, and people across vast distances in the opening months of Operation Enduring Freedom.

On January 9, 2002, her aircraft went down in Pakistan. All seven Marines aboard were k*lled. There was no battlefield glory in it, only duty performed far from home on a mission most people never think about. Her story is a reminder that sacrifice doesn't only happen in firefights — sometimes it happens on a routine flight, in service to everyone else.

“WE’RE GOING TO CRASH INTO THE GROUND! WE’RE OUT OF TIME!”  Chilling final cockpit recordings emerge as federal investigators identify 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha as the co-pilot aboard the doomed Learjet 60 that plunged over 32,000 feet per minute into Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board.

“We’re going to crash into the ground! ... We’re going to die! Holy f***, we’re out of time!”

Frenzied cockpit audio broadcast over Air Traffic Control frequencies seconds before ground impact

Key Details from the Crash Investigation
The Catastrophic Descent: Flight tracking data released by Flightradar24 indicates the twin-engine Learjet 60 (tail number N722BD) had departed South Florida en route to the Bahamas when it suddenly rolled past 60 degrees of bank and entered an uncontrolled vertical dive exceeding 32,000 feet per minute, erupting into a massive fireball upon impact in a roadway near Lantana.

Co-Pilot Identified: Officials and family members confirmed the first officer was 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha, an aspiring commercial aviator who fell in love with flying as a teenager, earning her private pilot’s license at age 17 while still attending high school before advancing through commercial multi-engine ratings.

All Nine Aboard Perished: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that both flight crew members and all seven passengers were killed instantly in the high-speed impact and resulting explosion. No ground fatalities were reported despite the crash occurring adjacent to commercial buildings.

NTSB and FAA Launching Full Probe: Specialized go-teams from the National Transportation Safety Board have secured the wreckage site to recover the cockpit voice recorder (CVR), inspect flight control surface actuators for mechanical jam or pitch runaway, and analyze engine thrust settings.

Technical Investigation Priorities
Assessing Sudden Loss of Control: Investigators are focusing on whether the high-performance business jet experienced trim runaway, structural failure, wake turbulence encounter, or an unrecoverable aerodynamic stall at cruising altitude.

Analyzing High-Altitude Flight Dynamics: The extreme reported descent rate of 32,000 FPM suggests the airframe was in a near-vertical terminal dive, pointing toward catastrophic system failure or total loss of pitch authority.

Crew Experience and Type Rating Review: The NTSB will examine pilot rest logs, aircraft maintenance records, and total turbine time in type for both flight deck crew members. 

RIP Nathalia Gadelha and the other members aboard.

Prisoners of war have tried everything to escape, but few plans were as patient — or as strange — as Benjamin Purcell's. Held in a North Vietnamese prison camp, the Army officer spent months secretly drilling tiny holes into his cell door, a little at a time, always watching for the guards. His early-warning system was a chicken he had trained to react whenever anyone approached.

On December 7, 1969, he slipped through the opening and spent nearly ten hours outside the wire — he even caught a bicycle ride toward Hanoi — before being recaptured and thrown into stocks for two weeks. He would not see freedom until 1973. He retired as a colonel, carrying one of the most remarkable escape stories of the Vietnam War: no tools, no help, just patience, nerve, and a chicken.

“POLITICIZATION IS PUSHING TROOPS TOWARD THE EXIT.” — A national survey of service members, veterans, and military families reveals that 53% of active-duty troops say increasing political interference and partisan polarization within the armed forces are driving them to leave service early—more than double the number citing pay or benefits.

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command, and you keep politics out of the mission. For too long, political leaders have treated the military as a partisan backdrop rather than protecting the core readiness of the force.”

— Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army Veteran & Executive Director of Common Defense

Key Findings from the National Survey
Politicization Outpaces Pay and Quality of Life: According to the latest national survey conducted by Common Defense, 53% of active-duty respondents report that growing political polarization makes them want to separate sooner, while only 5% say it encourages them to stay. By comparison, just 26% cited compensation and benefits as their primary retention concern.

Bipartisan Concern Across the Ranks: Frustration over politicization crosses traditional party affiliations. Among Republican-identifying service members and veterans, 72% agree that military families are being sidelined by political agendas, and 63% state defense policies are increasingly engineered for short-term domestic political gain.

Widespread Institutional Discontent: Over 79% of surveyed troops, veterans, and military dependents feel that civilian leadership and broader society are leaving the military community behind, with 74% expressing disapproval of how Congress oversees defense affairs.

Protecting the Apolitical Tradition: The survey highlighted strong opposition to using armed forces for domestic political functions: 55% of respondents reject deploying active-duty troops to monitor civilian polling stations or participate in domestic civil policing, reaffirming the constitutional standard of an apolitical military.

Strategic Implications for Retention & Readiness
Compounding the Recruiting Crisis: As all branches battle historically challenging recruiting environments, losing experienced mid-career NCOs and junior officers over political fatigue threatens institutional knowledge, unit cohesion, and technical combat capabilities.

Erosion of Public Trust: Decades of defense polling demonstrate that public confidence in the armed forces relies directly on its strictly non-partisan status. Partisan debates over command appointments, social messaging, and foreign policy rhetoric risk undermining that foundational trust.

Mission Focus vs. Narrative Battles: Frontline leaders emphasize that unit effectiveness hinges on warfighting competency, tactical drills, and equipment readiness, warning that culture-war distractions degrade morale in operational formations.

Honoring the memory and heroism of U.S. Marine Corporal Seamus M. Davey, an elite reconnaissance scout with 2d Force Reconnaissance Company (attached to 4th Force Recon Battalion).

On October 21, 2005, during combat operations in Abu Hyatt, Al Anbar Province, Iraq, Cpl. Davey's team entered an insurgent staging house and was ambushed at point-blank range—less than ten feet away—by four armed enemy fighters.

Struck by multiple rounds, Davey collapsed to the ground. Completely disregarding his mortal wounds and personal safety, he immediately brought his weapon to bear and opened continuous suppressive fire on the gunmen. His decisive, selfless actions drew the enemy's fire away from the doorway, allowing his fellow Marines to safely withdraw from the kill zone and survive. Davey continued to engage the enemy until he succumbed to his wounds, just three days before his 26th birthday.

For his extraordinary heroism, he was posthumously awarded the Bronze Star Medal with Combat "V" and the Purple Heart.

"Swift, Silent, Deadly." Semper Fidelis, Corporal Davey. Your brothers will never forget.

Staff Sgt. Jeffery M. Dawson earned the Distinguished Service Cross while deployed to Afghanistan with the 28th EOD Company (Airborne) in support of the U.S. Army's elite 75th Ranger Regiment.

Dawson said the mission in Afghanistan on Oct. 5, 2013, was supposed to be routine.

"That mission started out the same as every mission. The IED (Improvised Explosive Device) threat was low, and it was supposed to be a quick, easy target," said Dawson. "Upon infiltration, everything changed in minutes."

During the mission at a remote enemy compound, a fleeing insurgent detonated an explosive, killing himself and the team's multi-purpose canine Jani.

Dawson then realized that his team was surrounded by IEDs.

"Being the only EOD tech on the objective, it was up to me to clear medical personnel to the wounded and clear to all other personnel to get them to safety," said Dawson.

Despite being wounded by two separate explosions, Dawson halted the mission, disarmed the improvised explosive devices, and aided in the evacuation of dead and wounded Soldiers.

Navigating the chaotic situation in limited visibility for more than two hours, Dawson exposed himself to grave danger while locating three confirmed pressure plate IEDs and an additional six suspected devices, the award citation said.

"In any situation like that, you always revert back to training and stick with what you know," said Dawson, a Coalville, Utah native who has served in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Dawson said he was inspired by the dedication of his fellow Soldiers who braved the explosive-ridden battlefield to recover their fallen and wounded teammates.

"I remember looking around at all the devastation and seeing American flags draped over casualties in an effort to help keep them warm," said Dawson.

The staff sergeant said he was surprised to be put in for the medal, second only to the Medal of Honor.

"When I got back to camp, people were coming up to me and shaking my hand and hugging me telling me that they heard great things about me," said Dawson. "I kept thinking to myself that I was just doing my job

The Fort Bragg, North Carolina-based 28th EOD Company (Airborne) is part of the 192nd EOD Battalion, 52nd EOD Group, 20th CBRNE Command (Chemical, Biological, Radiological, Nuclear, Explosives), the only Defense Department formation that combats global CBRNE threats.

According to 28th EOD Company Commander Capt. Taylor J. Duren, his Soldiers conduct rigorous training to stay ready to jump out of airplanes and defuse explosive devices. Duren said his Soldiers regularly serve with the 75th Ranger Regiment, the U.S. Army's premier direct-action raid force.

"(The medal) highlights the relationship we have with the 75th Ranger Regiment since they are the ones who submitted (Staff Sergeant) Dawson's Distinguished Service Cross," said Duren.

Duren said the medal demonstrates the high caliber of the Soldiers serving in his one-of-a-kind company.

"What makes us truly unique is the level of professionalism each Soldier depicts in this company," said Duren, a native of Columbia, South Carolina, who has deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan.

"This award pays tribute to the level of training we put into the Soldiers hand-selected to serve in this company and their dedication to mission success," said Duren.

The heavy deep-strike missiles are integrated into Poland's HOMAR-K rocket artillery system, which pairs the K239 multi-caliber launcher with a domestically manufactured Polish Jelcz 8×8 heavy armored chassis and Poland's proprietary TOPAZ automated fire control network. The newly arrived ballistic missiles dramatically expand Warsaw's long-range deterrence across the Suwałki Gap and along NATO's eastern flank.

Hospital Corpsman Second Class Patrick Quill heard over the radio his MARSOC team leader was gravely injured. An IED exploded, wounding SSgt Christopher Antonik and setting off a complex Taliban ambush. As the team Corpsman, Quill completely ignored the intense fire and moved 150 meters through open terrain to reach Antonik's position. He put himself between the Marine and the enemy while applying tourniquets and dressings, then dragged Antonik 75 meters to the nearest cover. He worked to keep Antonik alive while the fight continued. A medevac bird finally arrived. Quill and another team member carried Antonik another football field away to load him on the chopper. Tragically, Antonik was too severely wounded by the blast and succumbed to his wounds. For his heroic selflessness and tireless effort to save the life of his team leader, Quill was awarded the Silver Star.

“Sorry, guys, I can't keep going.”

Those were the words of Lance Cpl. Brady A. Gustafson to the Marines in his vehicle as he was pulled away from his smoking machine gun minutes after his platoon was ambushed July 21, 2008, by withering enemy fire in Shewan, Afghanistan.

Nobody blamed Gustafson, 21, an infantryman with 2nd Platoon, Company G, 2nd Battalion, 7th Marine Regiment, for not being able to continue the fight, since the opening volley on the Marine mounted patrol included a rocket-propelled grenade that pierced the shell of the mine-resistant armor-protected vehicle in which Gustafson was manning the turret gun.

That RPG severed Gustafson's right leg, and yet he had the presence of mind to locate the enemy positions and place well-aimed machine gun fire on them, providing cover fire for the Marines in his platoon.

For his actions that day last year, Gustafson was awarded the Navy Cross and meritoriously promoted to corporal by Maj. Gen. Thomas D. Waldhauser, commanding general, 1st Marine Division, at a ceremony Mar. 27 at Lance Cpl. Torrey L. Gray Field at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms, Calif.
“What I like about today is that this is an opportunity to honor a Marine who had the humility, courage, presence of mind and camaraderie to keep going,” said Lt. Col. Richard D. Hall, the former commanding officer of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines,
while they were deployed to Afghanistan in support of Operation Enduring Freedom – noting that Gustafson was more concerned about the welfare of his brother Marines than his own safety.
“He represents what is best about the human spirit. You can't buy that kind of human altruism.”

The Navy Cross is the highest honor specific to the Naval services and the second highest award in the U.S. military. Gustafson is just the 18th Marine to earn the award since the beginning of the Global War on Terror.

The Marines of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines battled elements of Taliban and Islamist extremists in the Helmand and Farah provinces of Afghanistan.

Gustafson and Company G were patrolling in the village of Shewan, noted as a haven for insurgents, when they were ambushed from multiple positions by insurgents with RPGs and small-arms fire, according to the award citation for the Navy Cross.

After the RPG pierced the side of Gustafson's MRAP and struck him in the leg, causing the severe injury, he stayed focused and identified enemy firing positions, which he engaged with accurate machine-gun fire.

He noticed that the vehicle to his rear had become disabled by another RPG and instructed his MRAP driver to push the hobbled vehicle out of the “kill-zone.”

By doing so, Gustafson's MRAP became shrouded in fire. Through all this, Gustafson continued to direct fire at the enemy positions, suppressing their attacks and allowing the Marines to continue to engage the insurgents.

“Of every Marine I talked to, they all said if they had been hit in the leg with an RPG, the last thing they'd be thinking about is staying in the turret,” said 1st Lt. Andrew S. Bohn, 25, platoon commander of 2nd Plt., from Davis, Calif., and an occupant of the second vehicle that Gustafson directed to be pushed out of the line of fire.

Without that presence of mind, Bohn and the four other Marines from that vehicle may not have made it out of the ambush alive.

Only after firing more than 400 rounds, and reloading twice, did Gustafson permit combat aid-givers to remove him from the turret to apply medical treatment to his significant injuries. Lance Cpl. Cody Comstock, a member of Gustafson's platoon, applied his Combat Life Saver Course knowledge to the situation, wrapping a tourniquet around Gustafson's leg and dressing the wound while Gustafson was still in the turret.

“All of the lance corporals were going off their training in immediate action - nobody panicked,” said Bohn of his Marines. “There was a much-superior sized force attacking us, and there was only one (noncommissioned officer) in the platoon.”

After the action was over, Bohn recommended Gustafson for the Silver Star, the third highest combat award for valor, but Hall disagreed.

“My awards policy has always been strict (and) conservative,” said Hall, from Mankato, Minn. The former battalion commander noted that the deployment put all of his Marines in harsh conditions, and yet so many of the Marines excelled at operating at a high level that the “extraordinary became ordinary.”
Even so, Gustafson's actions were special.

“After reviewing what he did, even considering my awards policy and all the actions of 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, it was easy, to me, to submit his award as a Navy Cross,” Hall said.

Gustafson, from Eagan, Minn., has a long road to recovery and walks with a pronounced limp on his prosthetic right leg. The fact he suffered traumatic injury made his family even more grateful for his return.

“(The Navy Cross) is the icing on the cake for us, but we know that Brady didn't do this for the awards,” said Rick Gustafson, father to the Marine hero and an Air Force retiree. “We're very thankful we have him here today. That's our primary emotion.”

According to his parents, Gustafson intends to buy a home in his native Minnesota and attend college somewhere near home.

“He recognizes the importance and honor of the award, but at the same time, he feels funny about being recognized,” said Gustafson's mother, Kim, about her son's quiet, unassuming manner and reluctance to stand in front of the hundreds of Marines, guests and media at the ceremony. “He was just fighting for
his guys' lives."
